question: Inherited hyperammonemia is a result of deficiency of which enzyme of Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "N-acetyl glutamate synthetase deficiency" -> "decreased N-acetylglutamate" -> "reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I" -> "impaired urea cycle" -> "accumulation of ammonia" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Malate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Isocitrate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Succinate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
analysis: The urea cycle, also known as the Krebs-Henseleit cycle, is responsible for converting ammonia into urea for excretion. A deficiency in any enzyme of this cycle can lead to hyperammonemia. N-acetyl glutamate synthetase is crucial because it produces N-acetylglutamate, an essential activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme in the urea cycle. Without this activation, the urea cycle cannot proceed efficiently, leading to ammonia accumulation. The other enzymes listed (malate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and succinate dehydrogenase) are part of the Krebs cycle, not the urea cycle, and their deficiencies do not directly cause hyperammonemia. Therefore, the most likely cause of inherited hyperammonemia among the options is a deficiency in N-acetyl glutamate synthetase.
